cards.front: What does transcription do to a gene?
cards.back: It copies the gene's DNA letters into a single strand of messenger RNA (mRNA).
cards.quote: Key idea: In transcription, one gene's DNA letters are copied into a single strand of messenger RNA.
cards.section: Copy a gene into messenger RNA

cards.front: RNA has the base {{c1::uracil (U)}} in the place where DNA has thymine (T).
cards.quote: A, U, C, G (uracil, U, in place of T)
cards.section: Copy a gene into messenger RNA

cards.front: In transcription, which DNA strand does the enzyme read, and which strand matches the mRNA letter for letter?
cards.back: The enzyme reads the template strand. The coding strand matches the mRNA letter for letter, with T where the mRNA has U.
cards.quote: The other DNA strand, the coding strand, matches the mRNA letter for letter, with T where the mRNA has U.
cards.section: Copy a gene into messenger RNA

cards.front: A template DNA triplet reads GGA. Which mRNA triplet is made from it?
cards.back: CCU. G pairs with C, and DNA A pairs with RNA U. The mRNA pairs with the template, so its letters are not copied straight across.
cards.quote: pairing DNA A with RNA U, T with A, C with G, and G with C.
cards.section: Copy a gene into messenger RNA

cards.front: Where do transcription and translation happen in a bacterium?
cards.back: Both happen in the cytoplasm, because bacteria have no nucleus.
cards.quote: Bacteria have no nucleus, so both stages happen in their cytoplasm.
cards.section: Copy a gene into messenger RNA

cards.front: Why does a cell with a nucleus make an mRNA copy of a gene instead of sending the DNA itself to the ribosome?
cards.back: In cells with a nucleus, the mRNA copy carries the gene's message out.
cards.quote: In cells with a nucleus, that copy carries the message out.
cards.section: Copy a gene into messenger RNA

cards.front: A {{c1::codon}} is a group of three mRNA bases that means one amino acid or "stop."
cards.quote: Each codon, a group of three mRNA bases, means one amino acid or
cards.section: Read the message into an amino acid chain

cards.front: What is the usual start codon, and which amino acid does it stand for?
cards.back: AUG, which stands for methionine (Met).
cards.quote: AUG, the usual start codon, stands for methionine.
cards.section: Read the message into an amino acid chain

cards.front: In the standard code, the three stop codons are {{c1::UAA, UAG and UGA}}.
cards.back: The other 61 codons stand for amino acids.
cards.quote: In the standard code, 61 stand for amino acids, and three (UAA, UAG and UGA) are stops.
cards.section: Read the message into an amino acid chain

cards.front: Why are there 64 possible mRNA codons?
cards.back: Each codon has three positions, and each position can hold one of four bases: 4 × 4 × 4 = 64.
cards.quote: With four bases, there are 4 × 4 × 4 = 64 possible codons.
cards.section: Read the message into an amino acid chain

cards.front: Living things use about twenty common amino acids, yet there are 61 codons that stand for amino acids. What follows?
cards.back: Several codons can name the same amino acid.
cards.quote: Scope: several codons can name the same amino acid, not every gene codes for a protein

cards.front: A DNA template strand, written 3′ to 5′, reads TAC CAC CTT ATT. Using the codon chart (AUG Met; GUG Val; GAA Glu; UAA stop), what chain forms?
cards.back: Met – Val – Glu, then the chain ends. The mRNA is AUG GUG GAA UAA. The stop codon UAA adds no amino acid.
cards.quote: Pair each base: the mRNA is AUG GAG GAA UUU UGA.
cards.section: Read the message into an amino acid chain

cards.front: During translation, how does transfer RNA (tRNA) get the right amino acid into the chain?
cards.back: Each tRNA pairs with a codon through its three-base anticodon and brings the matching amino acid for that codon.
cards.quote: Translation check: A ribosome reads mRNA one codon at a time, tRNA brings each matching amino acid, and a stop codon ends the chain.
cards.section: Explore: transcribe, translate and mutate a gene

cards.front: The set of codon meanings, called the {{c1::genetic code}}, is almost the same in every living thing.
cards.back: A few exceptions exist, including in some bacteria and mitochondria.
cards.quote: The genetic code, the set of codon meanings, is almost the same in every living thing, with a few exceptions, including in some bacteria and mitochondria.
cards.section: Explore: transcribe, translate and mutate a gene

cards.front: A team put man-made genes for the two human insulin chains into E. coli and found the bacteria made the chains. What does this show about the genetic code, and why does it work?
cards.back: Bacteria can read a suitably prepared human gene. This rests on the rule that the genetic code is almost the same in every living thing, so a bacterial ribosome translates the same codons into the same amino acids.
cards.quote: In work published in 1979, a team put man-made genes for the two human insulin chains into E. coli.
cards.section: Explore: transcribe, translate and mutate a gene

cards.front: Young red blood cells fill with hemoglobin, while some pancreas cells make insulin. If both carry the same genes, how can they make different proteins?
cards.back: Specialized cells carry the same genes but use different ones.
cards.quote: Specialized cells carry the same genes but use different ones: young red blood cells fill with hemoglobin
cards.section: Explore: transcribe, translate and mutate a gene

cards.front: In the hemoglobin gene, the coding-strand triplet GAG changes to GTG. What changes in the mRNA codon and in the amino acid?
cards.back: The mRNA codon changes from GAG to GUG, so valine replaces glutamic acid.
cards.quote: One coding letter, GAG to GTG, puts valine in place of glutamic acid, and in low oxygen that hemoglobin can form rods that bend the cell.
cards.section: Evaluate: check your thinking

cards.front: A substitution changes one mRNA codon from UUU to UUC. Both codons mean phenylalanine. What happens to the chain?
cards.back: The chain is unchanged. A substitution can leave the chain unchanged when the new codon names the same amino acid.
cards.quote: A substitution can leave the chain unchanged, change an amino acid or create a stop.
cards.section: When one letter reaches a whole cell

cards.front: A substitution changes the mRNA codon GAG, in the middle of a coding region, to UAG. What happens to the chain?
cards.back: The chain ends early. UAG is a stop codon, so the substitution creates a stop and the chain stops at that point.
cards.quote: A substitution can leave the chain unchanged, change an amino acid or create a stop.
cards.section: When one letter reaches a whole cell

cards.front: One base is removed inside the coding part of a gene. What happens to the codons after it, and what often follows?
cards.back: All the later codons are grouped differently (a frameshift), so the chain changes from that point and often ends at an early stop.
cards.quote: A frameshift comes from adding or removing one base inside the coding part, and it often leads to an early stop.
cards.section: When one letter reaches a whole cell

cards.front: How do glutamic acid and valine differ in their behavior with water?
cards.back: Glutamic acid carries a charge and mixes well with water. Valine has no charge and avoids water.
cards.quote: Glutamic acid carries an electric charge and mixes well with water. Valine has no charge and avoids water.
cards.section: When one letter reaches a whole cell

cards.front: Why can sickle hemoglobin join into stiff rods when oxygen is low?
cards.back: Valine has no charge and avoids water, so it can fit into a water-avoiding patch on another hemoglobin. The molecules then join into rods.
cards.quote: When hemoglobin is low on oxygen, the valine can fit into a water-avoiding patch on another hemoglobin
cards.section: When one letter reaches a whole cell

cards.front: How many sickle alleles lead to sickle cell trait, and how many disease-causing copies are needed for sickle cell disease?
cards.back: Trait is one sickle allele with one usual allele, and it usually causes no symptoms. Disease needs a disease-causing change on both copies, at least one of them the sickle change.
cards.quote: Sickle cell disease needs a disease-causing change on both copies, at least one of them the sickle change.
cards.section: When one letter reaches a whole cell

cards.front: Newborn screens in 2010 found sickle cell trait in 34.1 per 1,000 newborns in Mississippi and 0.8 per 1,000 in Montana. About how many times higher is the Mississippi rate?
cards.back: 34.1 ÷ 0.8 is about 43 times higher.
cards.quote: Divide 34.1 by 0.8: the Mississippi rate is about 43 times the Montana rate, nearer fifty times.
cards.section: Use evidence: when is a mutation harmful?

cards.front: Newborn screening rates for sickle cell trait differ a lot between groups and places. Can those rows alone tell you why the trait is more common in some groups?
cards.back: No. They show a pattern, not its cause.
cards.quote: Can the newborn rows alone tell you why the trait is more common in some groups? No. They show a pattern, not its cause.
cards.section: Use evidence: when is a mutation harmful?

cards.front: Sickle cell trait lowered mild malaria risk by 50 percent and malaria hospital admission by 75 percent in Kenyan children. Using this, explain why the sickle allele can stay common in some places even though disease needs changes on both copies.
cards.back: Where malaria is common, one copy of the allele can protect against severe outcomes, so carriers can have an advantage. This rests on the rule that a mutation's effect depends on the protein and the environment, so it is not always harmful.
cards.quote: Protection was stronger against hospital admission (75 percent) than against mild malaria (50 percent).
cards.section: Use evidence: when is a mutation harmful?

cards.front: You test which kind of one-base mutation (substitution, insertion or deletion) most often changes a chain in a model gene. Why include a control, and what must stay constant?
cards.back: The control is the starting DNA translated with no mutation, so you know the normal chain to compare against. Keep the same starting DNA, one mutation per trial, the same codon chart, and only spots inside the coding part.
cards.quote: Control: translate the starting DNA with no mutation, so you know the normal chain.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: Two mRNAs make the same amino acid chain, but one lasts longer in the cell. Could the cell make different amounts of protein from them?
cards.back: Yes. Messages that make the same chain can differ in how long they last, which can change how much protein a cell makes.
cards.quote: two messages that make the same amino acid chain can still differ in how long they last, which can change how much protein a cell makes.
cards.section: Silent does not always mean identical
